newsitem.title: USA: Dlr retreats in US amid doubts over EMU timetable.
newsitem.headline: Dlr retreats in US amid doubts over EMU timetable.

text.p: The dollar ended a cross-driven U.S. session weaker against the yen and the mark on Friday amid growing doubts about Europe's plan to establish a single currency by 1999. Talk of a delay in the timetable for EMU spread through the market after Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said in a television interview that Germany might request a rescheduling of the start date to the monetary union. Though the German Finance Ministry later denied any plans to change the launch date, Prodi's comments weighed heavily on the market's psyche, sweeping the mark higher against the currencies of many of its European neighbors, particularly the Italian lira.

The lira fell to its lowest level against the mark in over three months, rising above the 1,000 per mark barrier despite reports that the Bank of Italy was actively selling marks for lire in an effort to defend its currency.

"All the excitement has been in mark/lira, and that seems to have triggered some mark buying which has pushed the dollar lower," said Rick Gomes, foreign exchange manager at Republic National Bank of New York.

The dollar ended at 1.6893/96 marks, below its opening rate of 1.6925/29. Overseas, the dollar dipped below the 120 yen level for the first time in a month, before settling in the U.S. at 120.12/22, down from 120.75/80 at the open.
Even as traders bought the mark against other European currencies, they sold the German currency against the yen, which benefitted from renewed hopes for a Japanese recovery.
Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita said in a speech on Friday that Japan's economy was recovering gradually and that the recovery was becoming firmer.
He also noted that Japanese private consumption was on an upward trend and a recovery in capital spending was spreading to many areas of industry.
Active buying of yen pushed the mark to its lowest level against the Japanese currency in eight months and also led the dollar lower against the yen.
Nevertheless, traders said they remain optimistic about the dollar's prospects over the medium-term.
"It's no reason to change the view that the dollar is going up," said Hans Boman, chief spot dealer at Swedbank, referring to Friday's weakness.
In other trade, the Mexican peso ended higher against the dollar after the U.S. government recertified Mexico as an ally in the war on drugs.
The peso had come under pressure earlier in the week on fears that U.S. decertification would hurt the Mexican economy.
The dollar ended at around 7.94 pesos, down from 8.00 pesos in early trade.

Elsewhere, the dollar ended little changed at 1.4773/78 Swiss francs against 1.4772/82 at the open. The British pound rose modestly to settle at $1.6280//90 against $1.6270/77 in early trade, and the dollar ended flat at Canadian $1.3680/85.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7785/90, up from $0.7756/61 at the open.
